453.t: Writing to Roosevelt and becoming a WPA conductor
453.s: Randolph wrote to the President, got an answer from Steve Early, and was assigned an A-1 conductor on the WPA music project.
453.q: Yes. That was during the WPA. And I got in the wind of this WPA and this big mammoth program was coming off. So I wrote to the President for the qualifications that I had and so on. I got a chance to be the supervisor of a union.

453.t: Building the WPA band from relief rolls
453.s: He began playing trumpet to fill the unit, recruited men from relief and then had the cream of the crop.
453.q: Well, when I first started, in order to keep the -- have the unit to operate, I had to play trumpet for a while, until I could get enough trumpet players so I could stand up and direct.

453.t: A swinging dance-band William Tell, played for Hal Kemp
453.s: The WPA dance band played Randolph's swing arrangement of William Tell, which Hal Kemp came to hear at noon.
453.q: Played so much trombone. And, well, I played such arrangements, like William Tell, I had Hal Kemp to come over -- I played a school and I had Hal Kemp to come way over -- he was playing in the city, and you know Hal Kemp's band.

453.t: Work schedule and monthly pay on the WPA project
453.s: Musicians played nights or rehearsed 9 to 1, and received a regular monthly income.
453.q: Yeah, you worked like this. If we played at night, we didn't rehearse in the day. But if we didn't go on a job and play at night, then we would have to

453.t: The WPA band is cut and Woody Herman sends a telegram
453.s: The project cut the jazz band while keeping the long-hair musicians, and the next night Woody Herman wired him to join; he stayed to about 1940.
453.ch: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
453.q: Well, I had that band -- oh, twice, because when they cut the band -- at least, cut the project, then my band, being the jazz band, then they cut it out, because they kept mostly all the longhaired musicians.

864.t: The WPA band directors, Gilbert and Martina
864.s: Gilbert classified the musicians by ability and built the band up; Martina replaced him and put out those who could not play.
864.q: I'm the one who got Lewis the man in the WPA band. In fact, I was the first trumpet player in the WPA band, could play anything that people could understand. There was a bunch of them in there. But Gilbert had the band then. Gilbert had the band way before Martina came. And what Gilbert did, he got…

864.s: He worked in a small orchestra with Joe and with all the city's brass bands.
864.q: Well, in the Depression, me and Joe, we were in an orchestra. We had, you know, our little outfits. And then, like all musicians, just playing with anybody high, you know. You had everything you could. And the Brass Band? Brass Band was the same way. I worked with all the brass bands in the city…

864.t: Playing in Garnier's band and the WPA band
864.s: Garnier was a regular member and director of the WPA band; Tillman got Louis Dumaine into it as first trumpet.
864.q: Yeah, I was a regular member. And then Garnier was my director in the WPA band. Oh, I see.

241.t: Living off music, wages and the Depression
241.s: Music was his only job and paid $55 to $70 a week; the WPA brought more entertainment.
241.q: Mr. Bill, I didn't have to do nothing but play music. I didn't do nothing but play. That's how I used to live off it then. You see, because everything was cheap. Well, we used to make our territory with the bill. We wouldn't make, in them days, we wouldn't make no less than $55, $60, $70 a week. No…

241.s: He never tried to join the WPA band.
241.q: No, I never did. No, I never went to that band at all. Never did. I didn't even try to get in it, you know what I mean? Yeah. So, and them cats had a racket in the house, you know what I mean? You know what I mean? Their friendship finished, you know what I mean?

241.t: Railroad shop, bridge work and painting during the Depression
241.s: He describes other jobs: railroad shop, concrete bridge work, and painting during the Depression.
241.q: I started painting for them in time of depression. So finally I painted for him and I painted for another part of this painting from Wonder Garden and all down there. And this kept me going. So after that, when the wall broke down, and I came back and I got a job, I come back in a railroad shop. So…

259.t: Bands after Red Island and through the Depression
259.s: After leaving Red Island he stayed with 'that day' about four years, then worked with a curtain man, John Cavan and Wooden Joe through the Depression.
259.ch: Liberty Band, marriage and the Depression
259.q: I stayed with that day about four years. Then after that I went with different bands, you know, but they didn't keep up long, you know.

259.t: Ninths before the Depression; leaving for Alexandria
259.s: Asked if ninths predate the Depression, he says yes, then recounts working in a big band in Alexandria and being tied by a debt.
259.q: With who? Before depression. When Cato? Depression. Say, when he started playing ninths, was that before depression? I just remember.

259.t: Who he played with when times got tough
259.s: The interviewer rephrases the Depression question as 'when times got tough'.
259.q: Who was he playing with when depression came on? When the what? Depression, depression. Depression. Depression. Depression. So who was you playing with when depression came? Depression, you say?

772.t: Switching to piano, Earl Hines, and returning to New Orleans in 1934
772.s: Banjos fell out of favor in the Depression, so he went back to piano in a band built around him, inspired by Earl Hines, then returned to New Orleans in 1934 and played odd jobs.
772.q: Because when, after I left that part of the country up there, and I came down there, it was around, getting around in the Depression time, and the people were putting the banjoes down for the ghettos. And I wasn't able to buy a ghetto, so I went back on the piano. And while I was before, while I…

772.t: WPA music project, port job, Joe Phillips band and Kimmel's Dixieland group
772.s: He was porter at the WPA music studio, then took a port job; his playing was limited, he joined Joe Phillips and Houston bands, and later Kimmel's group at the Paddock.
772.ch: Depression-era work and the day job
772.q: Oh, they were in the big band. No, I wasn't in the band. I never did get on, because it was late 40s and they was about to break the band. But I was the porter at the music studio down on Almonaster and Royal. They had a big building there. The teachers used to come there and teach the pupils. And…

772.t: Playing Basin Street and with Howard and Morgan in the 1930s
772.s: Back in the city he plays a cabaret on Basin Street and trips with Kid Howard, Isaiah Morgan and others.
772.ch: Depression-era work and the day job
772.q: Yeah, I played in there, with Willie and them. Well, I got right smart away, but still it wasn't enough to do any good. And it was a good while before guys knew that you were back in town. So I went on and I played around with Howard. Then I started going, making trips with Isaiah Morgan, with Sam…

956.t: The WPA band: first trombones, growth to 167 men, and its decline
956.s: He names the first 18 men and fellow trombonists, describes Martinez weeding out non-readers, the music-week parade, and why he left as the band shrank.
956.q: Or Sonny Henry? Sonny Henry came in after the band had been organized. Oh, maybe three months. But as the band progressed, they had 167 men in the band. Some could read and some couldn't read. So they said they was going to find out who could read and who couldn't read. So they sent old man Joe…

956.t: Rolling call of WPA band members by section
956.s: Henry lists the trumpets, reeds, rhythm and trombones in the WPA band, struggling over some names.
956.q: In the Reed section they had Wiesel Garman, Willie Umphrey, Joe Mitchell, the clarinets, and a fella by the name of the downtown. Can't think of that fella's name. From the clarinet? Oh, clarinet. Wasn't Joe Thomas, was it when they called him? No, no it wasn't Joe Thomas. I can't remember any real…

956.t: Leaving New Orleans, the Depression, and getting onto the WPA
956.s: Henry recounts his travels to Chicago, return in 1930, work at Tuskegee, and joining the WPA band via Bob Gilbert on the strength of his Chicago union cards.
956.q: how long it was before you came back and so on. Well, I left here in 19, early part of 19. I was 18, yeah. And I left here, went to Chattanooga. Chattanooga, stayed there a while. I went to Cincinnati. From Cincinnati, I went to Florida, just a floating plaster there. I wasn't playing no…

571.t: The Kingfish job with Billy and De De at a dollar a night
571.s: During the Depression Lewis worked seven nights a week at Decatur and Ursuline for about a dollar a night. He describes the band, Billy and De De marrying, and the rough crowd.
571.ch: Billy and De De Pierce at the Kingfish
571.q: Well during the, I started working with them during the Depression. Right there at Decatur and Ursuline, the Kingfish. That's where I worked with them. I worked there, and over two years, about two and a half years, close, for a dollar a night there. From eight to three in the morning.

571.t: WPA work and buying a metal clarinet
571.s: George worked WPA by day and played nights for a dollar, and bought a metal Albert-system clarinet.
571.q: Who played with you? Then besides that I waited. I was waking there for a dollar a night and Jeanette had been operating on it and I was waiting on the WPA. I'd catch the bus, the truck at 6 o'clock in the morning. I'd get off at 2 in the evening. I'd come in and work from 8.30 to 3 every night.…

571.t: Playing for low pay in Decatur Street joints in the 1930s
571.s: George recalls working for six bits and a dollar a night at the Kingfish, Mama's Place and others, and who played with him.
571.q: I worked for one job, I was just talking to my mother right there. Decatur, not my son, he's bringing me over here. Decatur, Toulouse, Decatur. And then there's a little Shaw Street coming from St. Peter. Wilkinson. Wilkinson. They had a saloon right on that corner. And I worked there one night…

909.t: WPA rules: daily practice, three-hour shifts and ending
909.s: Musicians had to report daily and were sent to three-hour jobs; Morris played nights with Rena, was caught, and went back to the riverfront.
909.q: Every day, yes. Practice every day. Every day, every day. And when you'd miss, that was a bad mock against you. They didn't want to know what's the trouble. If you get sick or something, you had to let them know.

909.t: WPA leaders: Louis Dumaine and Martinez
909.s: Dumaine directed the WPA band at first; the Washington boss Martinez checked the men's work; pictures to copy later.
909.q: See? That's the way that was. Now, if you go to either place, they're going to give every man his paper and tell him why they meet at. Just starting sitting at your time and knocking off sitting at your time. Well, that's the way that was. And the timekeeper would be there in his car and take your…

909.t: WPA band: Petoni headquarters and the Tulane Club
909.s: The big WPA band met at Petoni on Dumaine until drinking and check-cashing led authorities to move it to the Tulane Club.
909.q: Oh, we had a big band, yes. See, I'm standing up there. See, with that long tire, that's me standing up on that WPA band. Now, we used to play out there. And we used to go at Petoni there. That's why we had to meet there every morning.

229.s: Blakeney did not take part in the WPA but remembers WPA band concerts at the union hall.
229.ch: Central Avenue, WPA and the Alabam era
229.q: There's not much I can remember about the WPA, I didn't participate in the WPA too much because--I don't know.

229.t: Burbank pit and the Georgia Minstrels as highlights
229.s: He calls the Burbank Theater and the Georgia Minstrels tour highlights, and says Depression audiences still filled theaters.
229.q: So I recall that the highlight of my playing--of course I held some very important positions as a trumpet player, and one of those important positions was when I played at the Burbank Theater. I was there sixteen months in the pit.

229.s: Back in Los Angeles he plays small casuals for $17.50 a week, far below union scale.
229.ch: Hampton band, Honolulu and the war years
229.q: cians. Among those were Don Byas, who later became famous all over America and Europe. At that time I was back in Los Angeles playing casuals, small jobs at Depression wages.

242.t: Leading a WPA band and its personnel
242.s: He led one of two WPA bands, with Louis Dumaine leading the other; he lists Charlie Love, Manuel Paul and others.
242.q: Charlie Love. Yeah, Charlie Love was playing second trumpet in my band. I was playing first trumpet. See? Then they had a woman who was playing piano. She's a school teacher right now. Her name is Ruby. I forgot her last name. That's all I remember. And Joe Howell was playing sousaphone. And I…

242.t: How he got into the WPA band through his brother-in-law and Mr. Martinez
242.s: Brother-in-law Eddie Johnson brought him to sit in; bandleader Joe Martinez, a classical pianist, helped him get hired.
242.q: All right. Well, I'm going to tell you how to come to get in the band, you know? Yeah, go ahead. Well, at that time, they wasn't hiring anybody more in the WPA band because the WPA band was on their way, that is the whole WPA was on their way out because of what was it? Yeah. See? Okay. Because…

402.t: Another WPA band photo with about a hundred musicians
402.s: The interviewer notes the large WPA band picture and Sal praises its quality.
402.ch: Day job, band photographs and Chicago
402.q: Well, we had a good band, boy. We were drumming in that, man. Boy, Casper, Louis Voyages, the best, man. I mean, militant ships, you know? The best.

402.t: Playing for Roosevelt at City Park; the Mussolini march
402.s: Sal tells how the WPA band played at a Roosevelt visit and the Italian leader started a Mussolini march.
402.ch: Day job, band photographs and Chicago
402.q: I clapped it for Roosevelt, man. Fred Roosevelt. Oh. When they built the mall. Oh, get this kick, man. It blows fucking up in an open car with Governor Lash and Mayor May Street. This stupid band leader, Italian, starts playing the Mussolini march. I swear. I don't know how much of they was in the…

243.s: Breaux gives matinee and night-dance pay at the Tick Tock and general Depression prices, then they stray into Nicholson and other bandleaders.
243.q: You know, I think it's something people ought to know about the Depression. Well, for the matinee, you got, I think the matinee at that time was paying six bits, sometime a dollar. The night dance was down a quarter. Unless there didn't be a special dance, some club or another, well then you could…

243.t: Playing for nothing, 'cutting a ham', and hauling bass on the streetcar
243.s: Breaux explains the term for a dance with no customers, tells the Isaiah Morgan story, describes streetcar bass fares and mentions recording a trio session with Fats Pichon.
243.q: Bottom price? A lot of times nothing. I mean, it's just one of them things, man. You probably want to win.

255.t: WPA-stamped music and turning to the photographs
255.s: WPA-stamped sheet music prompts talk of the WPA band's music, and the group sorts out the photos.
255.q: Got all of that. They got all the cards. Yeah. We wanted to ask about this picture after a while, if you've got a minute to go over. Okay. Let's take your time. Thank you. Oh, yeah.

255.t: ERA band concerts at Jackson Square and public performances
255.s: The ERA band played weekend concerts, rehearsed at Patona, and split into groups for schools, parks and institutions.
255.ch: Brass bands and the ERA/WPA band
255.q: Well, they would cut them down, I'll tell you. And when this picture was taken out in the park at that time, they must have given us, some fella from New York must have given us $75 or something like that. They liked the band, but they would cut you down. And he would make you play and he would cut…

775.t: WPA band outside jobs, pay and hours
775.s: The WPA musicians could take outside jobs; Decatur Street work paid decently in the Depression and ran late into the night.
775.q: Down the corner. Down the corner of the night. That was plenty of money in that time. We were doing the depression. Uh-huh.

775.t: WPA-era band and the Kingfish Cabaret on Decatur Street
775.s: During WPA days he played with George Lewis and others at the Kingfish Cabaret and rehearsed in the large WPA band.
775.q: No, Billy, Billy, Billy, uh, piano, play the piano. Did he his wife? Billy, yes. Billy, Billy Pierce. Billy, Billy Pierce. That's the name of Billy Pierce. Yeah, that's right. Well, she was playing with us. So, after that, you know, before that, that, uh, I was playing in the WPA band. Now, one of…

765.t: The WPA bands and park concerts
765.s: WPA symphony, military and dance bands; Wednesday City Park concerts with jam sessions.
765.q: Well, some, but I mean he did a lot of reading most of them. He was really good. He got a good tone out of his violin. Oh, so many of them. I mean they had the symphony, they had the military bands, they had the dance band, and they had the recreation band with Cliff Curry. They had Pete Bacopa, he…

765.t: Golden Dragon, Silver Star, and the WPA band with blackface act
765.s: Trouble at the Golden Dragon, the Silver Star band, then the WPA bands and blackface park shows with Arthur Seelig.
765.q: Some place, I don't know, I'm kind of a little. Yeah. And then there was the Golden Dragon on St. Anne Street. Uh, the Slitko on piano, George Slitko, I haven't seen him for a long time. I think he was in California, he played a fine piano. Uh huh. And uh, we'll see Joe Stevens and myself, the…

857.t: Depression work and Buddy Petit, Deucey and Chris Kelly
857.s: Foster played anywhere he could in the Depression, never in the WPA band, and recalls Buddy Petit, Frankie Dusen and Chris Kelly.
857.q: No, never did. You never did? Never did play with that. Was always lucking up to having three, four nights job. Yeah. Didn't have to... Didn't have to bottom.

857.t: Matthews brothers and Depression pick-up bands
857.s: Brief talk of the Matthews brothers, then Foster lists places he played in pick-up bands as bands broke up in the Depression.
857.q: I think there's a bunch of, come on, Bill Matthews, Bibb Matthews, and Freeman. I think they got another one, I can't call his name.

192.t: Small Depression band with Bob Anthony
192.s: During the Depression he formed a small band that worked Delacroix Island dances.
192.q: Bob Antony. Bob Antony. Anthony. I don't know him. Yeah, I think he was, he spent a while in the United States Navy with us, but he was, went into TB sickness, was in the hospital for quite a while, right after he got out of the Navy. And he, we made, we used to play down.

192.s: He joined the ERA band, later the WPA band, working in it from 1933 until 1942.
192.q: Yeah, Louis Dumain. And I goes over there and had my labor card transferred from labor to musician, the old ERA band. And that's where we first started from the ERA band. We moved over to Tulane club and it's on the graphics between Roman and Bolivar.

886.s: He played three years in the WPA band, describing its directors, rehearsal and concert schedule and that it never played dances.
886.q: I was playing in the WPA band. I wasn't playing in my band. I was playing in WPA band three years. But on the WPA I was working. One client, one client player, one more. I was right there to see Mr. Morton.

886.t: Scuffling for work after the WPA
886.s: After the WPA he played street jobs, had no steady job and played on the radio.
886.q: I was playing in the street, a different band I loved. Sort of spotting, huh? Yeah, things were slow.

270.s: He names banjoists active when he returned, explains why he skipped the WPA band, and says he is freelancing.
270.q: Yeah, well, I got back in Chicago in 49. Yeah. Oh, yeah, Halston Verrett, he was still playing. George Gino was still playing. Mm-hmm. And, uh, uh, Fred Miner, we call him H.A. Miner, was still playing the banjo. And, uh, see, that's all. There was a terrific guy around here in the 30s, was named…

270.t: Peter Hone's society-circuit jobs and singer Harry Wells during the Depression
270.s: Hone's band holds country club and fraternity work and uses singer Harry Wells, in the Depression years around 1930-33.
270.ch: Desvigne, Chicago offers and Peter Hone's band
270.q: Yeah, I didn't get that. Alfred William on drum. drums. So Peter Hone had nice work like the field work like it is now playing like at the New Orleans Country Club. He had that tied up. Anything that was out there, he was a house band because they had a man named Mr. Crawford Ellis. That's the man…

298.s: A WPA band with two hours of rehearsal a day, concerts in parks, directed by Louis Dumaine.
298.q: That was a pretty good band. There was nothing to it, though. The only thing you'd go in the morning and rehearse about two hours and you was off the rest of the day. Unless they had a concert before you would go play somewhere. You'd go play a concert in the afternoon or concert at night. Well, I…

298.t: WPA pay and the three bands
298.s: Pay was $19 every two weeks; there were three bands, and he played in the seven-piece one.
298.q: What did he do? Used to play a metal phone. My every musician Ronnie was in the WPB band during that time. Wasn't nothing else but playing in the band. Get $19 every two weeks. You could live there, off $19.

801.t: Roosevelt, the CWA and regular band work again
801.s: Pay stayed a dollar until Roosevelt's election, when the CWA and similar programs brought regular band work at clubs for four dollars from eight to two.
801.q: Uh-huh. Until President Roosevelt got elected. And he started opening up with the CWA, all them different governing yards that put things back together. That's where the band started working regularly. E-Colony, New Horn, Poetry of Wern, Sender's Center, Lion Club, Boat Club, $4.00. And he was like…

801.t: Why he quit: the Depression and a dollar a night
801.s: Eddie says he quit around 1929 because of the Depression, when bands got a dollar a piece for nights lasting from 8 until morning.
801.q: I quit acting. Quit all of getting in the 40s. I mean, quit all of them. You didn't even play occasionally after the 1940s? No. I didn't go around them. I didn't visit them. I didn't do nothing. I stick to my son. I got mad. I raised my family. So I quit playing music. Now if somebody come hired…

858.t: George McCullum and the WPA band
858.s: Favorite musicians, then the WPA band that shrank from 135 men to 35, in which he played baritone saxophone.
858.ch: Brass bands and the WPA band
858.q: Ernest Rapania on drums. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And, uh, George McCollum, trumpet. Did you work much with him? Oh, yes. We're a WPA band. We've worked together for quite a few years. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

858.t: Sonny Henry, the WPA band and never having recorded
858.s: Sonny Henry in the WPA band, no recordings or film of that band, and Johnson never recorded.
858.ch: Brass bands and the WPA band
858.q: That's a shame. It's such a big band. Well, even playing for nothing is possible to you. There's a band that is working. It's playing for charity because we're going to steal the speech.

896.t: Small outfits during the Depression and the WPA band
896.s: He was not in the WPA band but played small outfits on guitar when the banjo was out, with young players who knew nothing of Dixieland.
896.q: wpa band was going on i was playing with a little small outfit different places here in town sometimes three pieces yeah four pieces a couple of young musicians just coming out you know yeah and knowing nothing much about no dixieland nothing about that that rock and roll play guitar or banjo i was…

896.t: Giving up music in the Depression and buying a guitar in the war
896.s: He sold his instrument in the Depression, bought a guitar in 1942 or 1943 and has played it since with Kid Thomas and others.
896.q: You gave it up? I had to give it up. I sold a band during... Oh, really? And have a during depression. Yes. We couldn't get anything to do. That's right.

825.s: More musicians worked during the Depression than ever, for a dollar to three dollars a night. When beer returned in 1933 small bands multiplied.
825.ch: Big bands, Depression work and the WPA band
825.q: No, that was during the Depression. During the Depression. Right. And matter of fact, they had more musicians working during the Depression than they ever did have. Because I mean, the odd of this, it was so rough, he was going playing for a dollar a night. Yeah. A dollar a night.

825.s: Ernie explains the rule that kept him out of the WPA band, the huge number of players and tests that weeded out poor readers. The band played at schools, hospitals and parades.
825.ch: Big bands, Depression work and the WPA band
825.q: Crab. Just give it to you like that. I'm telling you. In the Depression, the men that belong to these big bands, they weren't in that WPA band then.

574.s: He played in the WPA band during hard times.
574.q: Yeah, I played there a while. I played with them a while. I was in some tough days.

574.t: Ernest Milton's band and the Depression, 1933-37
574.s: He joined Milton about 1933-34 for three or four years; pay collapsed and he quit.
574.q: No, I wasn't playing with him. I got with him after that. I think I got with Ernest Milton on about 34. 33 or 34. Yeah, I was playing with Milton.

88.t: His father conducting a WPA band and giving lessons in Los Angeles
88.s: In Los Angeles his father, too old to break into jazz, led a WPA band at a playground and taught free lessons, buying instruments from Mike Gould.
88.q: No. See, now by the time we got here, what he did, you're talking about the WPA time now, okay? That's around '30,'31,'32 -- whatever year that was -- they had the WPA, but they also had WPA bands, and so over at one of the playgrounds, and he conducted -- the 22nd Street playground -- the band…

88.t: What the WPA band was and why it existed
88.s: Lee says the WPA band played band music and was a program to keep musicians and artists off the streets.
88.q: No, they played band music, you know, and like they tried to play -- well, I shouldn't say they tried to play, but you know, I was a young musician then and to me, that's just what I would have told you. That's what their music sounded like; they sounded like they were trying to play, but I mean,…

90.s: The government-sponsored WPA bands he heard rehearse, and gigs at Little Sam's in Black Bottom.
90.q: In fact, they still had WPA bands around during that period. WPA bands were bands that the government had sponsored, when President Roosevelt was bringing the nation out of the Depression. And WPA bands were...

90.s: Checking garbage cans before school, stamps for goods, and his song 'Hard Times In '29'.
90.q: And times were very hard, like, back during the Depression. We used to have to go and check out all the garbage cans before we'd go to school, to see if there was anything good in there worth using, like shoes or a shirt -- anything that you might be able to use, a pot or a pan or anything. Because…

383.s: Wilson recalls repeated predictions of jazz's death and his own starvation wages in 1929, with leaders blaming promoters for missing pay.
383.ch: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
383.q: obituaries for the jazz movement. There was one back in the fifties; in the forties when Duke and all the rest cut down the small bands -- you know, Basie went down to seven pieces, Goodman disbanded, and Dorsey quit. Back in the twenties, you know, jazz was swinging during the First World War, the…

383.t: The crash and talking pictures hit working musicians
383.s: Wilson and Hinton recall the 1929 crash, The Jazz Singer and theatre bandsmen losing jobs, and later meeting again in Chicago.
383.q: And of course, as far as making a living in music, the stock market crashed right about that time, and we were just in time to hear the musicians talking about how good times had been.

93.s: Green and his co-interviewer say tap was cheerful stuff that helped people forget the crash, with work plentiful on Broadway.
93.ch: Billy Pierce Studio and New York tap
93.q: You must remember now, in those times America was overcoming the stock market crash. See? They was trying to -- they was in the process of overcoming that.

93.s: Green says the country had to keep on its toes to overcome the Depression and theatres were a main outlet, so they did well.
93.q: Yeah. The whole country had to get on their toes, you know. To keep from thinking about the Depression. They was supposed to overcome the Depression. Like the series they've been having here recently, where the city went into some kind of budget disruption or something. Well, the Depression was…

384.t: Never out of work in the Depression
384.s: Morehouse worked straight through the Depression; Hutto credits NBC and CBS staff work, the first Hit Parade broadcasts and his versatility on vibes.
384.ch: Studio recordings of the late twenties and thirties
384.q: I don't know. I don't know why.

384.t: The Greystone's collapse and Charlie Horvath's bankruptcy
384.s: Virginia says her brother Charlie spent $160,000 renovating the Greystone, lost everything in the crash, and moved on to Cleveland and California.
384.ch: Bix, Trumbauer and the Goldkette sidemen
384.q: They used to come to Cleveland, with my brother. My brother was Joel. And he after the Greystone...I don't know if you want to record this stuff.

412.t: Chicago 1931-38: the Depression, radio, accordions and show business
412.s: Hodes says people first listened as an audience in New York in 1938, not Chicago. In Chicago he describes the lean years, with accordions, radio and the Depression pushing small bands out and agents demanding extra acts. They also touch on Louis Armstrong's struggles.

389.t: The Depression, King of Jazz and its Roxy flop
389.s: The picture was a bust and the Roxy show with Gershwin drew nobody, ending the band's good run.
389.q: So they went out and then they made the picture so I had nothing to do with it. I wasn't in it. I wasn't around when it was done, and they were doing, now, they're doing the Old Gold Show, doing them all from the road, and at the same time business is getting worse and worse and we have had the…

389.t: The radio show and the shrinking band
389.s: The Whiteman band was now on radio with Roy Bargy in front, records weren't selling, and the band shrank for the summer.
389.q: Well, at this time, you know, there's another thing. We're not making many records, we're doing a radio show and this is 18 to 20 numbers patterned after the Lucky Strike, B. A. Rolfe thing, this is 16, 18, 20 numbers an hour and you had to have the cuts, you had everything marked and at your…

13.s: Pay at the Grand Terrace depended on Ed Fox's take; he later had a day job.
13.ch: Joining Earl Hines and the Grand Terrace
13.q: Yeah. Things really got bad, you know. But I made it, you know. It was better than not working at all, you know.

13.s: Plenty of music, little money, still working.
13.ch: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
13.q: Roy was down at the Three Deuces. There was a lot of music going on. And Nance was downtown, you know, different places. Lot of bands out South. Wasn't making much money, but you were working.

172.t: Old pictures and the WPA band
172.s: He lacks old pictures and had quit before the WPA band.
172.q: Yeah, I did medicine. Who was that? I don't know. He didn't know the boy. No? I didn't. I just forgot it. And he asked me if I had that, I gave him something up on the music yet, man. And I said, come up there, we got out of my beer. And I gave him everything. I didn't want nothing to do with it.

920.t: The band in the 1930s and the Fort Worth Frontier Fiesta
920.s: Club dates through the Depression, the 1930s lineup, and the Fort Worth engagement with Nick, Tony and Robinson.
920.q: in the 30s yes uh where did you play we did various places uh not uh one engagement into the other but uh did various mostly club dates that was that was a lot of money in those days we'd work about three four nights a week or three nights a week in and out of town and that way we did fairly good…

175.t: Sidney Cate, the Moonlight Serenaders and Son Johnson
175.s: Son Johnson played with Sidney Cate's Moonlight Serenaders and a WPA band at Lemon Playground; local musicians rarely left home.
175.q: Very, he played alto saxophone and he played clarinet too. I can't think. Well he played, let's see, he was playing with the Moonlight Serenaders.

859.t: WPA band and the Chum Club with T-Boy
859.s: Gabriel names the musicians in his WPA-era band and at Babe Carous's Chum Club.
859.ch: Parade bands, instruments and the Eureka band
859.q: That's just to read. Oh, I read them. I mean a box with the reader. I'll get it out there. Anyhow, we played a record band. I played all around with T-Boy and me. We even played. We played the Chum Club. I can't exactly tell you. When I was in the WPA band I can't tell you what year that was…

150.t: Armstrong's 1931 benefit at the Army Base and Depression prices
150.s: A 1931 Louisiana Weekly notice of Armstrong playing a hospital benefit prompts talk of prices and hard times after the 1929 bank closures.
150.q: Because you got to remember the banks had closed in 1929. Hardly anybody had any money in 30 and 31. And that's when you had tokens on the market. You don't remember the little tokens. No, I'm not. If you spent 15 cents or 25 cents, you had to come up with a token. Then they had this thing about…

904.t: Vincent Lepresto's job, Depression pay and Richard M. Jones
904.s: Paul describes the cheap Lepresto job, Richard M. Jones taking over, and then joining Walter Johnson's band at the American Legion.
904.q: You see? And we're taking a job for a fella called Vincent Lepresto, a Paul Barnes band. Well we played for Vincent Lepresto through 33, and we were getting three dollars a night a man, and we would play two nights a week so that we made six dollars, and strange as it sounds, that six dollars was…

178.t: Depression years, the WPA band, his 1934 marriage and the return of beer
178.s: Ferbos played in the WPA band through the Depression, married in 1934 while with Pichon, and played with Handy when beer returned.
178.q: And even, well I know that because when we worked at the lake, I was newly married. And it's like when I was 18 I was newly married. That was before depression. In fact it was all building up, you know, but it wasn't definitely considered depression, you see, because when it really got there you…

181.t: Depression decline of brass bands; Onward band
181.s: Mac says funerals with bands fell off around 1932; Parker recalls Manuel Perez's Onward band with Bunk.
181.q: Oh, no. A lot of the fellas quit playing. There was no money but they made up right away.

250.t: Depression pay: 35 cents a night at open-air dances
250.s: Bergen says he never made money; in the Depression he played open-air dances near Spanish Fort for as little as 35 cents a night, meeting Charlie Storr there.
250.q: Oh yeah, we were playing at the Dharma Dance. It wasn't a prevelle, it was open air. I lived the second Spanish Forge, which location is now the Old Beach. Sometime we would make 35 cents a night. A fella named Ingehorn used to play with us out there. He was just starting with his metal clarinet.…

251.t: The Depression: 1934 job riots and the soup lines in New York
251.s: Albert was touring in 1934 but saw soup lines in New York and shared a cheap meal with Ben Barth.
251.q: No, in New York during the Depression, I've seen them on the soup line. And incidentally, Ben Barth, who had chosen universal attractions, he and I were close friends and we both shared a dinner together. In one of these soup lines, we bought a hamburger and a hot dog and a glass of wheat,…

871.t: Depression-era trio jobs at the athletic club and West End bungalow
871.s: Bigard recalls working with Walter Decou, Charlie Love and others at the Fifth Ward Athletic Club and a West End bungalow around 1930. Pay was a dollar and a half a night, nine to two.
871.q: Oh, I worked at Captain Petona, Fifth Wall Athletic Club. Yeah. Captain Petona used to own that. Mm-hmm. Who was that? And I worked with him over at West End Bungle for Old Man Albert Duboss. Yeah. And the band over there was Willie Paggio's on Trumpet. Mm-hmm. Old Man Sam Dutre, Sr. was on sax.…

257.t: No brass band experience; the WPA band
257.s: He never played in a brass band though he suggested one to Willie Pajeaud, and remembers the WPA band.
257.ch: Career, brass bands and choice of instrument
257.q: No Bill, I always wanted to, but it never to get a chance. I thought I had a chance one time when I gave a fellow out there, Joe Pazzo, I said, why don't you, maybe the city might be able to do something for y'all, you know. Yeah. And I said they got a fireman band, police band, might be able to do…

568.t: The Depression ends the music business
568.s: He lost everything in 18 months after 1928; music work vanished and he mentions Preston Jackson and a violinist who ran a sugar-place band.
568.q: We didn't have a dime. After 18 months, I didn't have a dime. Everything closed down after 1928. And musicians around here just like, whatever you say Preston Jackson, I always think about him. Because the boy was just in his primes, they're coming up, see. And he's got a wife, I don't know how…

186.t: The Depression and work for the band
186.s: Work continued but there was much less music during the Depression.
186.q: Who, Miles? Yeah. So I used to play when the Depression was, but they didn't get as much music to play, you know, as they did before. But they'd get some, but not as half as much, you know.

627.t: Eating pepper grass in hard times
627.s: Williams recalls chewing tough pepper grass for its juice when food was scarce.
627.ch: Williams on hard times and money
627.q: Sure. I have eaten, but it have grown out of season. It have run like a watermelon. And around, we have picked it and boiled it. It wouldn't get done. And eat that, drink the water off it, bite the bread. But we chew that, that, uh, Pepper Grace just like we chewing a cow chew a cud. You saw a cow…

83.t: Reel two opening; Depression food, red beans and cheap groceries
83.s: Reel two is announced, then Matassa explains growing up in a grocery during the Depression and how cheap beans and salt meat were.
83.q: Yeah. So, in that sense, I was really lucky. I was very lucky. But there was not a lot of sharing, a lot of caring. Families tended to take care of family, that kind of stuff. And my father and mother, I know, on occasion did what they could to help somebody that they knew needed help. Right.…

2.t: Never made much money; cheap collecting in the Depression
2.s: Russell earned just enough to eat and picked up records and sheet music very cheaply in the Depression.
2.q: No, I always made enough to eat on, and that's about all I ever cared for. I liked to have a few things. I mean the records I picked up, which would be invaluable to me, and other people too, which I wouldn't sell mostly at any price sometime when I was offered for them, even if I didn't have…

187.t: The WPA band under Professor Martinez
187.s: Martinez led a huge brass band favoring overtures; a trombone audition thinned it from 100 to 40 players, with names of members and small playing jobs.
187.q: I was in that, yes sir. Professor Martinez used to lead the band. And Lester Mayen was the leader when Martinez wasn't there. You know Mr. Martinez used to be piano player at the Sang-a-sale. He was a wonderful piano player. I saw some music that he wrote.

799.t: Big bands in the Depression, pay and Caprero's band
799.s: Why big bands survived the Depression, $35 a week as standard pay, and the Caprero band's personnel, including Grosso.
799.q: of that size working active in the country. That's right, it's all small band things now. Since the war, the trend has changed.

1008.t: The WPA band and the Fifth Ward Club
1008.s: Morgan played in the WPA band of about 119 players, rehearsing at the Fifth Ward Club on Dumaine Street.
1008.ch: Lessons, WPA band and sidemen years
1008.q: No, no. Somebody else told me that. The only band, a big band that I played in around that neighborhood, well we used to go and rehearse, so every day that was the WPA band.

875.t: Top band of the 1930s: Sidney Desvigne
875.s: Desvigne's band was the busiest in the Depression, with William Houston arranging.
875.q: Yeah, he was popular. Yeah, he was working. They would, they was playing all those top tunes. Somebody, I think Houston used to do most of the arranging for him at that time. He used to play the piano. Which Houston is that? The one that played the piano, William Houston.

475.s: Jobs paid about a dollar a night with tips during the Depression, but loving the music made it bearable.
475.q: A hundred himself. That's right. That's right. And I can get back to the subject. Oh yeah. Yeah I can remember certain jobs we played, I mean during those times I mean musicians played, they played a lot. But some of the jobs I mean you get on to a dollar a night. Oh yeah. Yeah we played for a…

590.t: Armstrong's money and popularity during the Depression
590.s: Discussion of whether Armstrong made good money in the Depression; he was a big name and records sold everywhere.
590.q: Well, I came up in the Depression. I know about the Depression. Well, was Armstrong making good money back then, during the Depression? Well, according to what things was happening at that time, you know? Good money was, I don't know what you would say called good money was-

190.t: Surviving the Depression with steady work; lending a horn to Cyril August
190.s: They say they always had work in the Depression, and the interviewer recalls lending a horn to the good player Cyril August.
190.q: During the depression, all the other, he always give me awake. Another father used to give me awake. Then the guys used to come high on me. I was waiting every night. That's right.

280.t: Hard times for musicians in the 1940s
280.s: Musicians earned little through the depression and early 1940s. Things only boomed after World War II.
280.q: In the 40s. Damn right, it was tough in the 40s. But I thought the depression... 39, 40s, man, things didn't get good until World War II, after World War II, 45.

282.t: Depression, injury, and joining Papa Celestin's band 1948-59
282.s: Music dried up in the Depression; after an injury and operation he joined Papa Celestin's band, staying until Eddie Pearson's era ended in 1959.
282.q: Oh, yeah. Well, that would be Sunday. Yeah. I mean, Sunday, that's the only time that they have parades, unless they have a day of funeral, you see. That was going to be a couple hours. You never put the music down? No, not completely, no. No. It went on like that and depression come on. It didn't…

778.t: Playing another boat; Lindbergh, the Depression and cheap food
778.s: She subbed once on the Capitol, was in New York at Lindbergh's flight and in New Orleans for the Depression.
778.q: Steamer Madison? I played one time on the Steamer Cap'n. I played more than playing piano on there, but he got sick one night and he had me to come to the place. He would just play for that. I wanted to ask you, where were you when Lindbergh crossed Atlanta? Where I was? I was in New York City…

404.t: Why San Jacinto declined, and cheap prices then
404.s: The club declined after the money was mismanaged and members died; prices in the 1930s were very low.
404.ch: Safe streets, decline and club life at San Jacinto
404.q: Well, on the last part of it, that's what I'm saying now, after that fellow had took the money, started messing with the money and it, you know, and it just went down and all the members, a whole lot of them died. This was more than that? Yeah.

284.t: Depression years and the WPA band
284.s: Work dried up in the Depression; he joined the WPA band, earning about nineteen dollars a week.
284.q: Yeah, well, after leaving that, after, after coming out of the sunny south band, well, I was, uh, telling the truth, it seemed like it was curtains for me cause I, I didn't care, I didn't worry about, too much about playing with it. And it was during depression at that time too. Yeah. That would be…

841.t: Funeral jobs during the Depression and low pay
841.s: They talk about who played with Allen and the few dollars a funeral or night paid in the Depression.
841.q: Uh-uh. I'm going to tell you the facts. I can't call back that for a man. The guy that's playing in the parade there.

878.t: Pay, tips, the Depression and the WPA band
878.s: They discuss low pay and no tips in the Depression, working for fun, and a white WPA band.
878.ch: Recordings, later jobs and changing times
878.q: We worked for peanuts. Yeah. But most of us worked though because we liked it. Of course that was guys who were single like myself. I loved it. I didn't make a lot of money but I had a lot of fun.

847.t: Depression pay and the big bands of the day
847.s: Sidney had more jobs than anyone; the most Jackson got was four dollars a night; many big bands then existed.
847.ch: Drum sets, small bands and the depression
847.q: But Sidney had more jobs than anybody else. He had the largest band around here and he was well known, well liked, and he was playing with the people like, so Sidney had more jobs than he could have at that time. Well, how much did they have to get for a date for one? Well, the most I got in…

288.t: Buying property, the 1929 crash and returning to Parks
288.s: He bought three properties in New Orleans, survived the Depression with his father-in-law's loan and developed land in Parks.
288.q: Dancing and everything else, you know what I mean. You see how second line followed? That's the way they did. And so when I'd get home I'd tell my wife, I'd say, the sooner I can give this thing up, I'd say the better. I'd say, because I want to play just for me and you if I can do what I want to…

633.t: Joining the Ninth Ward parade band under Gilbert and Martinez
633.s: Sonny Henry recommended him to the band; Gilbert tested players with sight music, Martinez took over, and he describes a rehearsal and the tune Delia.
633.q: A fellow by the name of Mr. Gilbert, you know. He had it in charge, so he said he's going to run a test. He run a test. He was going to run a test. And put the music up, you know. And the music wasn't all that hard. And a whole lot of fellows couldn't make, didn't know nothing at all. And a week or…

5.t: Last regular bands: Dickerson, Cook, Hines, WPA band and Zilner Randolph
5.s: After Hines the Depression cut work; he played in Norman Black's WPA brass band and finally Zilner Randolph's dance band.
5.q: Oh, yes. Well... Dickerson, others. Well, now after that, let's see, Dickerson and Charlie Cook. Now, I worked with Charlie Cook several times. I've... See, I think I went back with Dickerson, and then was back with Charlie Cook. See, I've moved them on those jobs several times. And then, uh, let's…

820.s: Frank recalls Johnny Beisdorfer's jazz band at Spanish Fort and his father's concert band, and the depression drought of work.
820.ch: Old bandleaders, drummers and Edgewater years
820.q: I remember Johnny Beisdorf. I played with him several, not steady, several incidental jobs. Uh-huh. But, uh, now all of this is on base. That's all after. Because when depression hit, I think I went about 14 months without a, with a $5 job.

290.t: The WPA band and not getting in
290.s: He quit about when the WPA band started; trying to get in was a matter of politics.
290.q: And that's the time you quit. That's the time you quit. Yeah, that was, by the round, about the same time I quit playing music.

291.t: Rejoining Oliver in 1931 and the Depression
291.s: He played New York night clubs, rejoined Oliver in 1931 and toured again in 1934-35 until Oliver's death, with little money.
291.q: Yeah we wasn't making any money during the depression. So that's the end of King Oliver because he passed away in 35. He never did recover. Oh no, he was very, very hurt. I know all the trumpet players I played with, they all were just like me. They're like my first time I played. You can ask me…

484.t: Spot work, then going broke in 1929
484.s: His sidemen played with him for spot work; steady engagements came only with the Depression. He lost his money in 1929 managing Atlanta's Con Corporation, then went back to New Orleans.
484.ch: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
484.q: Oh, we better not mention brands on here.

766.s: After 1930 he played many jobs in Buras and Venice, where clubs had no names.
766.q: I played several different jobs, I mean. It's hard to think of them, played so many of them. I went down to Buress a long time.

306.t: Whitewashing tombs in the St. Louis cemeteries and the hard times of c. 1929
306.s: Rene worked whitewashing tombs in St. Louis cemeteries, paying permits to the priest.
306.ch: Hard times and working bands of the 1930s
306.q: We used to whitewash tubes. Yeah, we used to whitewash tubes. Didn't tell you that either. No. Some do, yeah. That much work? Wow. Yes, sir.

708.t: Away from nightclubs until 1934; the tea room and the piano
708.s: She stopped nightclub work after about 1927 and returned by 1934. During the Depression she and her husband ran a tea room where touring musicians played their piano.
708.q: Well, I tell you, after, that wasn't directly after I left the casino that I went. See, when I, after I quit there, I didn't work no more until about, in the nightclubs anymore until about, about, uh, let's see, what year was it I started back? That was 27. I didn't start back anymore until about…

440.t: Depression and Prohibition atmosphere in Chicago
440.s: Hard times, jazz ignored in dance halls, the New Deal, and the South Side.
440.q: It’s funny, I always thought to myself that I was there in the worst time and I never really realized it. It’s probably because I wasn’t there before it. And it was hard. And of course it was hard. I took it for granted that it would be hard. Jazz was playing in The Subway, which opened at ten at…

323.t: The Depression: work, scale and radio pay
323.s: Plenty of work in the 1930s; Yorkville gigs, union scale, and WINS pay of eighty-five dollars.
323.q: No. No that’s a good question but it didn’t. It didn’t. There was a lot of work. Club work, bar mitzvahs, night clubs, outdoor parties, whatever. And all the radio stations had a band, even if it was a six piece band. And the networks all had 65 men except WOR, they had 45. The Don Lee Network. But…

163.t: The Depression and the family's lost real estate savings
163.s: Family money in real estate was lost by 1933, but they kept some buildings and rent was covered.
163.q: Yeah, as a matter of fact. So we’re talking about — well it didn’t really hit them until about I think it must have been ‘33, ‘34, ‘32. The crash was 1929. They had their money in real estate, and it took about — and he made good money, he had a Cadillac and he had a raccoon coat and all that. But…

1.t: The Depression hits the South first
1.s: Barker describes the Depression's early impact on New Orleans, then wanders into factories, Japan and the moon landing before returning to New York in 1930.
1.ch: Professional start and leaving New Orleans
1.q: You got that? We was talking about the states and the music business. The poor people in the South and the rich people in the South feel effects of a depression before them people in the great big cities. When I got to New York in 1930, there was talk of a depression. It actually hadn’t hit New…

142.t: Conducting the Tropicana orchestra for meals; the depression
142.s: He played for free and conducted the Tropicana show orchestra for food for a month, while the enforced idleness was meant to depress and warn him.
142.q: For meals, yea. The food situation in the country was horrible in those days. (About the same as right now) So, and still today there is a trumpet player Guerido Elarvarde, he still play for years at the Tropicana just for food. At night, he go play the show, for the food. So, I play that and I…

471.s: Cobb recalls cheap groceries and cigarettes sold by the penny.
471.ch: Growing up and learning drums in Washington
471.q: I guess I was too young to remember it. I just remember they didn’t have food stamps or nothing like that. I remember you could go to the store and buy $5 worth of groceries and have to have somebody help you bring it back, because the dollar was worth a lot of money. I remember cigarettes being 15…

108.s: Playing 1920s and 30s music for Keillor is hard and reminds him of the Depression.
108.q: I don’t know. I haven’t really given much thought to that. I try to roll with the punches. Whatever it is, I try to follow the concept of what it is and try to play it as best as I can. I’ve had no problem with it. It doesn’t disturb me to do that. I’m sure there’s some music that, if it were older…

4.s: Musicians on WPA earned about twenty-five dollars a week to rehearse and play in parks; Spikes was refused because he owned property.
4.ch: Central Avenue clubs, Nordskog, Sheffield and Music Town
4.q: Well, all the musicians on WPA. They paid 'em, I think, uh, I don't know, twenty...twenty-five dollars a week to re... you rehearsed all...every morning two hours, and then on Saturday you played in a park or somewhere a couple of hours. But that was...that was a...generally, that kept you livin',…

9.t: Depression days and landladies who trusted him with rent
9.s: He lived through the Thirties with little money, owing rent to people who believed in him, and he repaid every debt.
9.q: Because at that time, them were some tryin' days, what we're talking about now, way back in the Thirties. Them were tryin' days, believe me. Nobody had anything, and there was no work, people weren't working. It was terrible! Nobody had anything. Money just wasn't here. You had apple lines. You…

89.t: Depression gigs and the Arcadia Ballroom with Charlie Turner
89.s: The early depression paid seven dollars a gig until he landed a job at the Arcadia Ballroom with Charlie Turner.
89.q: Oh, yes, my. In the '30's, the very first part of '30's was a little rough because business was dying down and the big bands were struggling to hang on.

28.t: Kept by a woman: apartment, pistol, tailored suits and a gold horn
28.s: She moved him into an apartment with a sunken tub, gave him a pearl-handled automatic and suits, and he recovered his own horn from Blunt, as the Depression arrived.
28.ch: Newark and first years in Harlem
28.q: I took a second look and forgot all about Mr. Blunt into the love action. I said I need to go to school now. So I went down and went in. So she said, well, yes. You need an apartment. Well, everybody was living (inaudible) apartments, had those sunken bathtubs at that time, that was something else.…

452.t: Cheap food then and the falling dollar now
452.s: Cobb recalls four-cent sausage and three-cent bread, and the talk turns to the dollar being worth 26 cents and the pointlessness of saving.
452.q: But I want to say this to you, Stanley: During that time, you could go out if you want pan sausage, you could get it for four cents a pound. Get a loaf of bread for three cents. And we could get five pounds of pan sausage on the corner at the corner grocery store for 20 cents and feed a lot of…

120.t: Broke in Chicago after leaving Meroff
120.s: Having saved nothing, he finds little work in 1931, some bosses cannot pay, and he lands a job in a burlesque theater.
120.q: Yeah - in '31-- And, so, here I am back in Chicago and I checked in a hotel and I-- of course, with all thatmoney I made, I didn't save any--- I always figured - tomorrow is another day. So, then, I found the picking a little tough right now and I even jobbed around in places where the boss would…

418.s: A short continuation noting times were rough, with the early Thirties pretty bad in the South.
418.ch: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
418.q: Well, I don't know about the Twenties. I know the early Thirties was pretty bad down there. The next time we come together I'll tell you about it.

99.t: Oklahoma in 1931, deep Depression and Sy Oliver leaves
99.s: The band plays Oklahoma and Arkansas dances for little money; Sy Oliver leaves and Peanuts falls ill in Okmulgee.
99.q: So we left and went on out to Oklahoma. We played a little ballroom in Oklahoma City, we played a ballroom in Tulsa, we played several dances in Tulsa and around Tulsa, and things just never -- never got better.

169.t: Bernie Young's WPA band in Milwaukee
169.s: He joins Bernie Young's WPA band in Milwaukee, finds its members just draw pay and do not work.
169.q: : Yeah. See, all of the band was on that. So when I joined it, I went there, they didn't give a shit about working. You know, they was workin' anyway! So I'm there, and I ain't got no money and I ain't got no job... I mean, I got a job but they don't work!

19.t: Joining Tommy Miles's WPA band and writing Opus 403
19.s: The WPA arts project recruits Tommy Miles's band; Malachi writes his first big-band piece, named after the 403 dismissal slip.
19.ch: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
19.q: But all the while this was going on, I was playing jobs at night with older musicians. For a long time when I worked around Washington, I was the youngest musician in the band. After the stint that I had with Jelly Roll Morton up there at the Jungle Inn, I think I made... I got a little band of my…

74.t: Earl Roberts, the Showboat and the Depression
74.s: The manager from Massachusetts cannot find good jobs as the Depression sets in, and the band breaks up.
74.ch: Trent's band: touring, sidemen and breakup
74.q: right down into Oklahoma. He booked us down in Oklahoma, we played two nights at the Oklahoma Ballroom where we played before; we played long engagements. This is with Earl Roberts and he just couldn't get any more good jobs, couldn't get me any more good jobs and the Depression had started.

149.s: The Depression barely touched him; the president gave him a gold trumpet.
149.ch: Band family, war years and wrap-up

30.t: The Ellington sound on radio and working through the Depression
30.s: You could tell it was Ellington within seconds on radio, and the band worked everywhere through the Depression while others starved.
30.q: Well, you take like in those days, I mean, in the radio time when there wasn't TV, you know, there were bands on the radio. Well, you could tell it was Duke's band the minute he got on the radio because it's a complete different style of arrangements and music, the way he had it all cut up and…
